latin: Per modum legendi sine punctis in lege, et modus scrıbendi res diuinas, et unialis continentia per indeterminatum ambitum rerum diuinarum, nobis ostenditur.
translation: By the manner of reading without points in the Law, the manner of writing divine things, and the unified containment of divine matters through an indeterminate range, are shown to us.
translation_note: 'Unialis continentia per indeterminatum ambitum rerum diuinarum' is the thesis's crux. Wirszubski glosses it as meaning that 'the underlying unity and continuity of divine revelation admit of endless variations of meaning' (wirszubski1989:9272).
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch21, from Latin at farmer1998:27932
doctrine: The thesis concerns the textual form of the Torah rather than a single point of Kabbalistic detail. Farmer's note states that to read Hebrew 'without points' (vowel signs) effectively removes divisions in the text (farmer1998:28012). Wirszubski argues that because an unvocalized consonantal text can be read and combined in more than one way, the thesis's 'unialis continentia per indeterminatum ambitum rerum divinarum' means that 'the underlying unity and continuity of divine revelation admit of endless variations of meaning' (wirszubski1989:9272), which he connects to the Rabbinic maxim, quoted by him, that "The Torah has seventy faces" (wirszubski1989:9272).
historiography: Wirszubski marks this as the point at which Pico's Kabbalistic conclusions turn from points of detail to the Law as a whole: "All the theses considered so far touch upon points of detail. The seventieth concerns the Law as a whole" (wirszubski1989:9243). He states, of the thesis's central phrase, "This is in fact what to my mind Pico means by 'unialis continentia per indeterminatum ambitum rerum divinarum'" (wirszubski1989:9272). The excerpt consulted then begins a further sentence, "No other thesis brings out Pico's awareness of", which breaks off there (wirszubski1989:9272).
